power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Time is foundational to social life, yet Social Representations Theory has often treated it as the background against which representations change, rather than as a dimension of meaning-making in its own right.

This theoretical review distinguishes processual dynamics (how representations emerge, stabilize, circulate, and transform) from temporality: how past, present, and future are socially and symbolically constituted.

From here, it examines structural, dialogical, sociodynamic, and genetic approaches in order to trace how these traditions have engaged with the past through narratives, memories, and histories, and with the future through projects, expectations, and anticipations.

The review shows that all four traditions contain temporal assumptions, but that the field has developed fuller accounts of how the past organizes the present than of how possible futures orient collective life.

Drawing together conceptual resources already present within the theory, we propose a re-temporalization organized around four components: temporal contents, representational processes, projects, and projections.
This agenda treats time as symbolically constructed, experientially lived, normatively encoded, and politically distributed.
It enables research to examine how groups negotiate temporal pace, direction, reversibility, and legitimacy, and how unequal capacities to define the past and the future shape representational life.
Re-temporalizing SRT therefore deepens the theory's concern with common-sense knowledge by linking continuity and transformation to the politics of memory and anticipation.

In Émile Durkheim's (1915) formulation, time constitutes a paradigmatic collective representation: an abstract and impersonal framework that transcends individual consciousness and organizes collective existence.
text.formatted: In Émile <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Durkheim's (1915)</ref> formulation, time constitutes a paradigmatic collective representation: an abstract and impersonal framework that transcends individual consciousness and organizes collective existence.

text.text: Temporal categories, in this view, are socially produced yet relatively stable, embedded in ritual and institutional life.
The shift from collective to social representations proposed by Serge Moscovici (1961) fundamentally alters this picture.
text.formatted: The shift from collective to social representations proposed by Serge <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Moscovici (1961)</ref> fundamentally alters this picture.

text.text: Representations are no longer unified and stable social facts.
Even the most consensually shared -what Moscovici (1988) termed hegemonic representations-remain historically situated and open to contestation.
text.formatted: Even the most consensually shared -what <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Moscovici (1988)</ref> termed hegemonic representations-remain historically situated and open to contestation.

text.text: They circulate across differentiated public spheres, rather than standing above them (Jovchelovitch, 2007).
text.formatted: They circulate across differentiated public spheres, rather than standing above them <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Jovchelovitch, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: This shift has important implications for how time is understood within representational processes.
If collective representations are tied to enduring structures, social representations are embedded in communicative dynamics.
They are continuously reworked through media, institutional debate, and everyday interaction.
In this perspective, representations are not fixed entities but processes in transformation (Marková, 2008).
text.formatted: In this perspective, representations are not fixed entities but processes in transformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Marková, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, while some approaches within Social Representations Theory (SRT) have developed explicit temporal sensibilities, the status of time remains unevenly theorized.
This limitation is not unique to SRT.
Across social and psychological theories, time is often treated implicitly as a background dimension against which social processes unfold (Martins, 1974; Nowotny, 1992).
text.formatted: Across social and psychological theories, time is often treated implicitly as a background dimension against which social processes unfold <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Martins, 1974;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Nowotny, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: As Prosser (2025, p. 2) notes, social psychology still captures "a snapshot of human life that is in motion", leaving how time itself becomes meaningful relatively unexplored.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr">Prosser (2025, p.</ref> 2) notes, social psychology still captures "a snapshot of human life that is in motion", leaving how time itself becomes meaningful relatively unexplored.

text.text: However, a growing body of research shows that meaning-making processes concerning the past and the future are central to present social life (Michaelian & Sutton, 2017) and culturally embedded (Sircova et al., 2014; Stolarski et al., 2018).
text.formatted: However, a growing body of research shows that meaning-making processes concerning the past and the future are central to present social life <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Michaelian & Sutton, 2017)</ref> and culturally embedded <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(Sircova et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">Stolarski et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these developments highlight the need to clarify how time is conceptualized and mobilized within SRT.
In this article, we address this need by distinguishing between two analytically related but non-equivalent dimensions.
On the one hand, processual dynamics refer to how representations emerge, stabilize, and transform.
On the other, temporality concerns how time itself is socially and symbolically constituted within the everyday sphere.
While SRT has extensively developed the former, the latter often remains implicit in empirical research.
As a result, time frequently appears as a background condition within which representational processes unfold, rather than as a dimension or object of representation in its own right.

Building on this distinction, we will first examine how time is addressed across different approaches to SRT (structural, genetic, sociodynamic, dialogical), asking to what extent it is treated as a background condition or explicitly addressed as a dimension or object of representation.

text.text: Then, we will focus on how empirical research engages with the past (through narratives, memories, and histories) and the future (through projects, expectations, and anticipations), exploring how these engagements reveal different temporal openings within the theory.

This mapping serves a twofold objective: first, to clarify how time has been conceptualized within SRT; and second, to specify what is gained by treating temporality as a constitutive dimension of meaning-making.

These two movements converge in the discussion, which advances a re-temporalization of SRT by outlining future research directions grounded in a theoretical definition of temporality that is more fully integrated into the theory's own conceptual resources.
The following sections examine how different traditions within SRT address time.

The distinction between structural, sociodynamic, genetic, and dialogical approaches is adopted here as a heuristic framework, rather than as a strict taxonomy of authors or schools, as it reflects a consolidated way of organizing theoretical orientations within the theory (e.g., Sammut et al., 2015; Lo Monaco & Rateau, 2025).
text.formatted: The distinction between structural, sociodynamic, genetic, and dialogical approaches is adopted here as a heuristic framework, rather than as a strict taxonomy of authors or schools, as it reflects a consolidated way of organizing theoretical orientations within the theory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Sammut et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Lo Monaco & Rateau, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, many scholars initially associated with one approach have progressively expanded their theoretical scope, particularly to engage more directly with issues of history, development, and temporality.
We treat these expansions as evidence of SRT's internal pluralism rather than departures from it.
Accordingly, the aim is to examine how time is variously taken for granted, implicitly structured, or explicitly problematized across different approaches to SRT.

In doing so, we distinguish between processual dynamics -well established within SRT-and the more limited ways in which time itself becomes an object of representation or a dimension of meaning-making.
The structural approach (Abric, 1987 (Abric, , 1994) ) embeds a distinctive orientation toward continuity, in which representational stability takes precedence over transformation.

text.text: By distinguishing between a central core of historically sedimented meanings and a peripheral zone of adaptive elements (Moliner & Abric, 2015), it frames social knowledge as a system that endures across generations while selectively absorbing novelty.
text.formatted: By distinguishing between a central core of historically sedimented meanings and a peripheral zone of adaptive elements <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Moliner & Abric, 2015)</ref>, it frames social knowledge as a system that endures across generations while selectively absorbing novelty.

text.text: This view aligns with broader cognitive perspectives emphasizing the economization of resources and the pursuit of coherence and cognitive consonance (Festinger, 1957; Heider, 1946).
text.formatted: This view aligns with broader cognitive perspectives emphasizing the economization of resources and the pursuit of coherence and cognitive consonance <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Festinger, 1957;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Heider, 1946)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this orientation, social representations have been described as possessing "some stability over time… between conscious cognitions and the longue durée of collective mentalities" (Bauer, 2015, p. 79).
text.formatted: Consistent with this orientation, social representations have been described as possessing "some stability over time… between conscious cognitions and the longue durée of collective mentalities" <ref type="bibr">(Bauer, 2015, p. 79)</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, time is primarily a dimension against which continuity and change are described.
Change is conceived as gradual and accumulative, proceeding through peripheral adjustments that, as far as possible, preserve the integrity of the core (Wagner et al., 1996).
text.formatted: Change is conceived as gradual and accumulative, proceeding through peripheral adjustments that, as far as possible, preserve the integrity of the core <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">(Wagner et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Although subsequent refinements have acknowledged phases of emergence, stabilization, and transformation (see for instance Wachelke, 2011 , or Moliner, 2016), these developments largely extend the analysis of processual dynamics without explicitly problematizing time; transformation remains predominantly reactive, typically triggered by contextual disruptions that pressure the system to recalibrate (Flament, 1994).
text.formatted: Although subsequent refinements have acknowledged phases of emergence, stabilization, and transformation (see for instance <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Wachelke, 2011</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">, or Moliner, 2016)</ref>, these developments largely extend the analysis of processual dynamics without explicitly problematizing time; transformation remains predominantly reactive, typically triggered by contextual disruptions that pressure the system to recalibrate <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Flament, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, the core is defined primarily by its resistance to change.
It comprises a limited set of beliefs that remain stable and around which strong group consensus is organized (Abric, 1994).
text.formatted: It comprises a limited set of beliefs that remain stable and around which strong group consensus is organized <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abric, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Core elements simultaneously perform meaning-making, ordering, and stabilizing functions: any alteration at this level therefore implies a potential reconfiguration of the representation as a whole and, by extension, a disturbance of the social bonds it sustains (Moliner, 2016).
text.formatted: Core elements simultaneously perform meaning-making, ordering, and stabilizing functions: any alteration at this level therefore implies a potential reconfiguration of the representation as a whole and, by extension, a disturbance of the social bonds it sustains <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Moliner, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Peripheral elements, by contrast, operate as conditional buffers.

They absorb contextual variability and shield the core from direct confrontation with disconfirming experience; they are historically situated, draw on biographical experience, and remain negotiable among social groups (Flament, 1994; Wagner et al., 1996).
text.formatted: They absorb contextual variability and shield the core from direct confrontation with disconfirming experience; they are historically situated, draw on biographical experience, and remain negotiable among social groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Flament, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">Wagner et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: The peripheral system is also closely tied to behavioural schemas that orient conduct in concrete situations, thereby mediating between representational meaning and situated practice.

Representations and practices engage in an ongoing interaction, and contradictions in action become the primary trigger of representational adjustment (Quenza, 2005). Flament (1994) further argues that representational change hinges on whether new practices are seen as reversible, legitimate, and justified, leading to different degrees of core restructuring.
text.formatted: Representations and practices engage in an ongoing interaction, and contradictions in action become the primary trigger of representational adjustment <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">(Quenza, 2005)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Flament (1994)</ref> further argues that representational change hinges on whether new practices are seen as reversible, legitimate, and justified, leading to different degrees of core restructuring.

text.text: While, these formulations introduce temporal distinctions (e.g., reversibility, anticipation), they remain anchored in the regulation of change rather than in an explicit theorization of temporality as such.
In this context, the notion of the zone muette (Abric, 2005) acquires particular significance.
text.formatted: In this context, the notion of the zone muette <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Abric, 2005)</ref> acquires particular significance.

text.text: Traditionally defined as those cognitions available to individuals but left unexpressed under ordinary conditions (Guimelli & Deschamps, 2000), this "silent zone" emerges because articulating such contents could challenge moral or normative values upheld within the group (Chokier & Moliner, 2006).
text.formatted: Traditionally defined as those cognitions available to individuals but left unexpressed under ordinary conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Guimelli & Deschamps, 2000)</ref>, this "silent zone" emerges because articulating such contents could challenge moral or normative values upheld within the group <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Chokier & Moliner, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: These unspoken elements embody a form of inertia, reflecting meanings sedimented in the history of the group.
At the same time, the silent zone constitutes a latent site of change: when sociosymbolic conditions shift, dormant elements may resurface, unsettling the apparent stability of the representation.
Continuity thus appears as an ongoing negotiation between stabilization and transformation, in which what is silenced remains available for reactivation.
A related opening is identified in what Abric (2005) termed the zone des éléments contrastés.
text.formatted: A related opening is identified in what <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Abric (2005)</ref> termed the zone des éléments contrastés.

text.text: Often detected in Free-Association studies, this domain includes contents mentioned by relatively few participants (low frequency) but attributed high subjective importance (low rank).
These contrastive elements express divergent or minority viewpoints within the group and may signal the presence of subgroups organized around alternative value configurations.

While marginal, they introduce a limited opening within the otherwise conservative architecture of the model: transformation may emerge from the periphery when minority positions accumulate symbolic weight or become more publicly legitimate.

However, recent empirical work comparing social representations across cohorts indicate that stability in central elements may coexist with variation in peripheral meanings, pointing to gradual differentiation over time (Fasanelli et al., 2020; Moreira et al., 2023).
text.formatted: However, recent empirical work comparing social representations across cohorts indicate that stability in central elements may coexist with variation in peripheral meanings, pointing to gradual differentiation over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Fasanelli et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Moreira et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These findings introduce a diachronic perspective in which different generations may organize and prioritize meanings differently around the same object, enabling the study of change and persistence as jointly observable.

Taken together, the structural approach recognizes the relevance of context, practices, and latent zones of potential transformation, yet it ultimately conceives social representations as systems oriented toward the preservation of established meanings.
Change is primarily reactive rather than anticipatory.
In this sense, time is not explicitly theorized but functions as an implicit condition of continuity, within which stability is maintained and transformation is regulated.

The approach therefore offers a detailed account of processual dynamics -how representations stabilize, adjust, and occasionally restructure-while leaving largely unexamined the question of temporality properly speaking: how time itself is socially and symbolically constituted within the everyday sphere.

The dialogical approach (Marková, 2000 (Marková, , 2003 (Marková, , 2023) ) offers one of the most explicit engagements with time within SRT.
text.formatted: The dialogical approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Marková, 2000</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Marková, , 2003</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Marková, , 2023) )</ref> offers one of the most explicit engagements with time within SRT.

text.text: It conceptualizes representations as ongoing dialogical processes unfolding across past, present, and anticipated future positions.
Representations are never formed in isolation; they emerge through exchanges with real, remembered, or imagined others (Marková, 2003; Jodelet, 2014).
text.formatted: Representations are never formed in isolation; they emerge through exchanges with real, remembered, or imagined others <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Marková, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Jodelet, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In this sense, processes of representing are intrinsically temporal, as they carry traces of prior discourses while orienting toward possible responses.
Dialogical subjectivity is inherently multi-positional and multi-voiced.

The Self is constituted through the continuous interplay between internalized and external perspectives, including those of concrete interlocutors, social groups, institutions, and imagined audiences (Marková, 2008).
text.formatted: The Self is constituted through the continuous interplay between internalized and external perspectives, including those of concrete interlocutors, social groups, institutions, and imagined audiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Marková, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Time, from this standpoint, refers to the lived organization of experience, in which past trajectories, present engagements, and future orientations coexist within a polyphony of voices.
The self is thus always engaged in dialogue with an "inner alter" that reflects socially and symbolically mediated perspectives (Marková, 2003).
text.formatted: The self is thus always engaged in dialogue with an "inner alter" that reflects socially and symbolically mediated perspectives <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Marková, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: This dialogical engagement is not only backward-looking, drawing on shared histories, or present-focused, negotiating current positions, but also anticipatory, insofar as it unfolds within relations that orient participants toward possible futures of interaction and understanding (Marková, 2023).
text.formatted: This dialogical engagement is not only backward-looking, drawing on shared histories, or present-focused, negotiating current positions, but also anticipatory, insofar as it unfolds within relations that orient participants toward possible futures of interaction and understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Marková, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Imagination plays a central role within this dynamic (Marková, 2018).
text.formatted: Imagination plays a central role within this dynamic <ref type="bibr">(Marková, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: From a dialogical perspective, imagination is not an isolated mental faculty but is intrinsically intertwined with communication, meaning-making, and memory.
In this sense, imagination emerges through the dynamic relations between Self and Others, across temporal horizons of past, present, and future.
It may involve moments of distancing from immediate experience, yet it also remains embedded within the ongoing flow of socially mediated thinking and interaction.
Dialogical imagination therefore

A further mechanism central to dialogical theorizing is that of themata: fundamental antinomies (e.g., self/other, continuity/change, responsibility/blame) that structure common sense and re-emerge in moments of social tension (Moscovici & Vignaux, 1994; Marková, 2017).
text.formatted: A further mechanism central to dialogical theorizing is that of themata: fundamental antinomies (e.g., self/other, continuity/change, responsibility/blame) that structure common sense and re-emerge in moments of social tension <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Moscovici & Vignaux, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Marková, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Themata link historically sedimented oppositions with present controversies, becoming particularly visible when established interpretive frameworks are destabilized.

Empirical studies show how such oppositions organize public sense-making across domains such as risk, migration, and political conflict, connecting collective memory with anticipations of possible futures (Smith et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Empirical studies show how such oppositions organize public sense-making across domains such as risk, migration, and political conflict, connecting collective memory with anticipations of possible futures <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">(Smith et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Through themata, dialogical processes articulate affective, moral, and temporal dimensions of representation.
Despite this strong emphasis on temporality, dialogical approaches have been subject to internal critiques regarding their treatment of stability, power, and constraint.
For instance, Boulanger and Valsiner (2017) argue that the approach may underplay how representations sediment into relatively stable forms that guide action implicitly.
text.formatted: For instance, Boulanger and <ref type="bibr">Valsiner (2017)</ref> argue that the approach may underplay how representations sediment into relatively stable forms that guide action implicitly.

text.text: Without sustained attention to vagueness, absence, and indeterminacy, dialogical analyses risk reintroducing a static ontology of representations under a dynamic vocabulary.
From this perspective, temporality should be understood not only as processual unfolding but as structured by asymmetries, constraints, and partially stabilized meanings.
These limitations become particularly evident in contexts shaped by institutional and political asymmetries.

For instance, Caillaud et al. (2020) show that dialogical exchanges are embedded within material, institutional, and discursive arrangements that unevenly distribute authority and delimit what can be said, by whom, and with what consequences.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Caillaud et al. (2020)</ref> show that dialogical exchanges are embedded within material, institutional, and discursive arrangements that unevenly distribute authority and delimit what can be said, by whom, and with what consequences.

text.text: Consequently, the presence of multiple voices does not guarantee equal recognition or influence over future-oriented meaning-making.
Rather, dialogue may reproduce dominant representations by constraining how alternative voices are positioned and received.

Recent dialogical extensions further foreground time through the analysis of imagined futures. Pedersen (2021) shows how dialogical impasses can emerge when competing social representations project incompatible futures.
text.formatted: Recent dialogical extensions further foreground time through the analysis of imagined futures. <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Pedersen (2021)</ref> shows how dialogical impasses can emerge when competing social representations project incompatible futures.

text.text: In such cases, breakdowns in dialogue are not reducible to past misunderstandings but to conflicts over which futures are considered viable or legitimate.
At the same time, these future orientations are unevenly distributed across social positions, as different actors have unequal capacity to define and sustain particular trajectories.
This highlights how time can become a dimension of representational struggle, rather than merely a background for processual dynamics.

Taken together, the dialogical approach makes temporality more explicit within SRT by conceptualizing representations as polyphonic processes in which past, present, and future are dynamically articulated.

At the same time, while dialogical approaches theorize the negotiation of meanings in considerable detail, they pay less attention to how understandings of the past and the future themselves become contested objects of representation.
The distinction between dynamics and temporality remains, even here, only partially drawn.

The sociodynamic approach (Doise, 1980; Doise et al., 1999; Clémence et al., 2014) conceptualizes social representations as structured by social differentiation and positioning rather than assuming uniform consensus.
text.formatted: The sociodynamic approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Doise, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Doise et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Clémence et al., 2014)</ref> conceptualizes social representations as structured by social differentiation and positioning rather than assuming uniform consensus.

text.text: Its central proposition is that representational diversity emerges from the articulation of distinct but interdependent levels of analysis: intraindividual, interindividual/situational, positional, and ideological (Doise, 1980; see also Doise & Valentim, 2015, for a recent extension of the model).
text.formatted: Its central proposition is that representational diversity emerges from the articulation of distinct but interdependent levels of analysis: intraindividual, interindividual/situational, positional, and ideological <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Doise, 1980</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Doise & Valentim, 2015,</ref> for a recent extension of the model).

text.text: These levels are not sequential but mutually conditioning: meaning-making is simultaneously organized through interaction, shaped by social positions, and regulated by ideological and normative frameworks.

From the perspective adopted in this review, the sociodynamic approach does not explicitly theorize temporality; rather it offers a differentiated account of how time is implicitly structured across levels of analysis, without theorizing it as a dimension of representation in its own right.

At the intraindividual level, the focus lies on how individuals organize their perceptions and evaluations of the social environment through cognitive and motivational processes shaped by prior socialization (Doise, 1980).
text.formatted: At the intraindividual level, the focus lies on how individuals organize their perceptions and evaluations of the social environment through cognitive and motivational processes shaped by prior socialization <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Doise, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: Time remains implicit and is primarily reflected in processes of consolidation and reorganization of cognitive structures, rather than being treated as an object of representation.

At the interindividual and situational level, processual dynamics are the central analytical concern. Doise (1980) characterizes these dynamics as spiral rather than strictly linear, suggesting that interactional tensions may intensify, transform, or reconfigure across sequences of exchange.
text.formatted: At the interindividual and situational level, processual dynamics are the central analytical concern. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Doise (1980)</ref> characterizes these dynamics as spiral rather than strictly linear, suggesting that interactional tensions may intensify, transform, or reconfigure across sequences of exchange.

text.text: This perspective is consistent with the socio-psychological tradition of cognitive development developed by Doise and Palmonari (2010), where representations are produced within interactional sequences in which positions are negotiated, stabilized, or destabilized.
text.formatted: This perspective is consistent with the socio-psychological tradition of cognitive development developed by <ref type="bibr">Doise and Palmonari (2010)</ref>, where representations are produced within interactional sequences in which positions are negotiated, stabilized, or destabilized.

text.text: Meanings are therefore produced within ongoing dynamics of coordination and conflict between groups; accordingly, anchoring and objectification are treated as socially positioned operations, governed by normative and ideological principles (Clémence, 2001; Clémence et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Meanings are therefore produced within ongoing dynamics of coordination and conflict between groups; accordingly, anchoring and objectification are treated as socially positioned operations, governed by normative and ideological principles <ref type="bibr">(Clémence, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Clémence et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: At the positional level, representational differences reflect structured social affiliations -such as class, profession, institutional role, or political orientation-which are historically constituted and relatively durable.

Here, time is tied to the persistence and transformation of social positions across trajectories: representational patterns endure insofar as the structures that sustain them persist, and change when these structures are reconfigured (Doise, 1980).
text.formatted: Here, time is tied to the persistence and transformation of social positions across trajectories: representational patterns endure insofar as the structures that sustain them persist, and change when these structures are reconfigured <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Doise, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: At the ideological level, continuity is maintained through normative and value systems that regulate the interpretation of social positions and conflicts. Doise (1980) describes this level as providing metasystems that structure the dynamics occurring at other levels.
text.formatted: At the ideological level, continuity is maintained through normative and value systems that regulate the interpretation of social positions and conflicts. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Doise (1980)</ref> describes this level as providing metasystems that structure the dynamics occurring at other levels.

text.text: These frameworks display relative continuity across episodes of contestation, while also allowing limited reconfigurations in the interpretation of social arrangements.

In this sense, the ideological level introduces a limited opening toward anticipatory dimensions, as political and normative frameworks often imply projections about desirable or undesirable collective futures.
Crucially, these levels are articulated rather than independent.
Transformation occurs when articulations between levels are reconfigured: for instance, when shifts in social positioning alter interactional dynamics, or when ideological principles are challenged.
Time in the sociodynamic approach is therefore multilevel and conjunctural: it is structured differently across levels and emerges through their articulation..
Taken together, the sociodynamic approach offers a differentiated account of how time is structured across levels of social organization and conflict.
However, it only partially opens toward temporality as an explicit object of representation.
What remains untheorized is how actors across these levels represent time itself: as urgent or deferred, as progressive or cyclical, as a resource distributed unequally across social positions.

This gap is not incidental; it reflects the approach's constitutive focus on the synchronic organization of difference rather than on the symbolic meanings through which groups orient themselves toward past and future.

The sociogenetic approach (Duveen & Lloyd, 1990; Duveen & de Rosa, 1992) situates representational change within the organization of time across social life.
text.formatted: The sociogenetic approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Duveen & Lloyd, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Duveen & de Rosa, 1992)</ref> situates representational change within the organization of time across social life.

text.text: It understands social knowledge as continuously produced through the interplay between individual development, social interaction, and collective meaning making.

Representations are therefore examined across three intersecting processes which articulate situated interaction, individual development, and broader historical transformation rather than forming a simple sequence of temporal scales (Psaltis, 2015a).
text.formatted: Representations are therefore examined across three intersecting processes which articulate situated interaction, individual development, and broader historical transformation rather than forming a simple sequence of temporal scales <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">(Psaltis, 2015a)</ref>.

text.text: Studying these processes requires attention to how representations are constructed in interaction, appropriated across the life course, and circulated and transformed at the societal level.

Methodologically, this orientation has been associated with the combination of longitudinal designs, interactional analyses, and documentary, policy, or media analysis to examine change across these scales (Flick et al., 2015; Negura et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Methodologically, this orientation has been associated with the combination of longitudinal designs, interactional analyses, and documentary, policy, or media analysis to examine change across these scales <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Flick et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Negura et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Microgenesis refers to the situated construction of representations in interaction.
It captures the processes through which social identities and the representations that sustain them are elaborated and negotiated in real time (Duveen & Lloyd, 1990).
text.formatted: It captures the processes through which social identities and the representations that sustain them are elaborated and negotiated in real time <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Duveen & Lloyd, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: The focus here is on the present in the making: representations are co-constructed, stabilized, or revised through discourse.

Microgenesis functions as the immediate condition of both ontogenesis and sociogenesis, insofar as broader representational fields are reproduced -or occasionally transformed-through situated encounters (Duveen & Lloyd, 1990; Psaltis, 2015a).
text.formatted: Microgenesis functions as the immediate condition of both ontogenesis and sociogenesis, insofar as broader representational fields are reproduced -or occasionally transformed-through situated encounters <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Duveen & Lloyd, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Psaltis, 2015a)</ref>.

text.text: While interaction often reproduces taken-for-granted meanings, it can also generate ruptures in which implicit assumptions become explicit and open to reworking (Psaltis, 2015b). Wagner et al. (1998), for example, showed how representations of the public sphere in Brazil emerged through everyday exchanges among citizens, politicians, and media actors, linking civic identity to competing moral evaluations of the nation.

text.text: Ontogenesis brings time to the level of the life course, tracing how individuals appropriate and transform shared meanings through experience and socialization.
Ontogenetic processes describe how people grow into already existing representational fields while also potentially reshaping them (Flick et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Ontogenetic processes describe how people grow into already existing representational fields while also potentially reshaping them <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Flick et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Biographical time thus constitutes the site where broader sociogenetic transformations become psychologically real.

A classical line of research has therefore focused on developmental studies examining how social representations are constructed, stabilized, and transformed through the articulation of microgenetic interaction, ontogenetic development, and sociogenetic structures.

Within this tradition, development is understood not as the internal maturation of isolated cognitive structures, but as a socially mediated process in which identities, power asymmetries, and forms of communication shape both learning and representational change (Duveen & Lloyd, 1990; Psaltis, 2015b).
text.formatted: Within this tradition, development is understood not as the internal maturation of isolated cognitive structures, but as a socially mediated process in which identities, power asymmetries, and forms of communication shape both learning and representational change <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Duveen & Lloyd, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Psaltis, 2015b)</ref>.

text.text: Research in Cyprus illustrates this dynamic particularly clearly.

Decades of ethnocentric history education embedded opposing national narratives so deeply that they structured memory, political expectations, and attitudes toward coexistence among both Greek Cypriots and Turkish
Cypriots (Makriyianni & Psaltis, 2007).
text.formatted: Cypriots <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Makriyianni & Psaltis, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Following the opening of checkpoints in 2003, cross-group contact reduced prejudice in both communities, but in ways that differed depending on participants' biographical starting points (Yucel & Psaltis, 2020).
text.formatted: Following the opening of checkpoints in 2003, cross-group contact reduced prejudice in both communities, but in ways that differed depending on participants' biographical starting points <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">(Yucel & Psaltis, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The same historical turning point was therefore taken up differently across individual life trajectories.
Finally, sociogenesis concerns how representational fields are shaped by collective, geopolitical, and historical transformations (Duveen & de Rosa, 1992; Sibley et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Finally, sociogenesis concerns how representational fields are shaped by collective, geopolitical, and historical transformations <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Duveen & de Rosa, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Sibley et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: It focuses on how representations circulate within societies, interact with institutional discourses, and are reconfigured across historical contexts (Flick et al., 2015; Carugati & Selleri, 2011).
text.formatted: It focuses on how representations circulate within societies, interact with institutional discourses, and are reconfigured across historical contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Flick et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Carugati & Selleri, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Sociogenesis is therefore not a distant macro layer but an ongoing historical process that becomes visible in situated meaning making (see for example Negura, 2021).
text.formatted: Sociogenesis is therefore not a distant macro layer but an ongoing historical process that becomes visible in situated meaning making (see for example <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Negura, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Building on Duveen's sociogenetic framework, subsequent work has explicitly tracked representational change across multiple scales, proposing "genetic social psychology" as a continuation and expansion of this legacy across developmental and cultural research (Psaltis, 2015a (Psaltis, , 2015b;; Psaltis & Wagoner, 2026; Zapiti & Psaltis, 2012).

text.text: The core premise of this framework is that all objects of knowledge are pre-signified by social representations and ideologies that pre-exist individual subjects and condition their knowledge potential (Castorina, 2017).
text.formatted: The core premise of this framework is that all objects of knowledge are pre-signified by social representations and ideologies that pre-exist individual subjects and condition their knowledge potential <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Castorina, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, time is organized across interrelated scales: meanings circulate between the immediacy of social encounters, the biographical trajectories of individuals, and broader historical transformations.

Over time, scholars working within the genetic tradition have increasingly incorporated dialogical themes to better account for how actors navigate present positions, emerging tensions, and possible futures (Gillespie, 2006; Gillespie & Cornish, 2010; Psaltis & Wagoner, 2026; Zittoun, 2019).

Beyond Schools of Thought: SRT through Past and Future The four approaches outlined above offer distinct ways in which SRT has engaged with time: structural continuity and reactive change, dialogical articulation of past, present, and future, sociodynamic differentiation across levels of social organization, and genetic articulation across developmental scales.
However, several research strands cut across these approaches, substantially extending how time is addressed within the theory.

Drawing on adjacent traditions -most notably memory studies, narrative psychology, and cultural psychology-this literature examines how the past is narratively constructed and how future orientations are anchored in collective meaning-making.
The following sections trace these developments, beginning with SRT's engagement with the past and showing how it already implies a future orientation.

Work on the past within SRT extends and reinterprets its core mechanisms of anchoring and objectification, foregrounding how representations draw on prior meanings while being reworked in relation to present concerns.
Within this field, three interrelated strands -memory, narrative, and history-offer complementary ways of examining how time is made meaningful in social knowledge.
Some perspectives emphasize continuity and endurance, while others foreground rupture, contestation, and the moral tensions involved in representing the past.
Drawing on Bartlett's (1932) social theory of memory, Moscovici (1988) noted that "very ancient beliefs lurk in the shadows" and continue to shape representational life (p. 244).

Yet the past is not only recalled; it is narrated.
Narrative approaches show that remembering involves structuring events into meaningful sequences.
As Bruner (2011) argues, narrative constitutes a mode of thought that organizes experience through plots connecting beginnings, developments, and outcomes.

Monuments, memorials, and commemorative sites materialize historical narratives in public space, stabilizing dominant accounts or inviting critical reflection on past destruction and future responsibility (Brescó de Luna et al., 2023; Zittoun, 2004).

text.text: Representations of history are thus continuously negotiated and reworked across changing social positions.
Across these contributions, the past emerges not as a fixed repository but as a dynamic resource mobilized in relation to present concerns.
Remembering stabilizes identity and continuity, but it also opens space for reinterpretation and contestation.

In this sense, engagement with the past already implies a future orientation: if representations draw on prior meanings to make sense of the present, they also contribute to shaping how possible trajectories are imagined and negotiated.
If memory and history ground SRT in continuity, research on the future foregrounds its projective and imaginative dimensions.
Rather than treating anticipation as a derivative of remembering, this body of work shows that future orientations are central to representational life.
SRT is particularly useful here because it treats anticipations not as individual attitudes, but as socially shared meanings anchored in collective practices and identities.

Making this contribution explicit requires, however, a sustained distinction between processual dynamics -how representations change over time-and temporality as a lived, symbolically constituted horizon of expectation.

The theoretical foundations of this distinction can be located within SRT itself. Bauer and Gaskell's (1999) Toblerone model embeds anticipation as a temporal axis, connecting memory and project within a single representational structure.

text.text: Future-oriented imagination is thus structured by the semiotic resources available to each group, making it both a site of conflict and a potential locus of convergence.
Cultural psychology approaches complement this view by conceptualizing social representations as symbolic resources through which individuals and groups navigate uncertainty.

Valsiner (1999, 2001, 2003) situates representations alongside language, narratives, images, rituals, and artifacts as semiotic tools that enable actors to project alternatives beyond the immediate present.

text.text: Building on this perspective, Zittoun and Gillespie (2018) conceptualize imagination as a looping process in which individuals temporarily decouple from the present, mobilize symbolic resources to explore distal spheres of experience, and return transformed -a mechanism that is both individually enacted and socially scaffolded.

text.text: Empirical illustrations of this process show how symbolic resources are mobilized across contexts: Gillespie (2006) demonstrates how tourists construct idealized selves through imaginative engagement with culturally available meanings, while Zittoun (2019) shows how shared narratives enable communities to project possible futures for their landscapes.

text.text: Within this broader framework, Brescó de Luna (2018) introduces the notion of prolepsis to account for a more explicitly temporal mechanism: imagined futures are brought into the present by shaping how the past is narratively reconstructed, thereby orienting collective action.

Relatedly, Jovchelovitch and Hawlina (2018) show that utopian thinking functions as a collective semiotic guidance system capable of mobilizing transformative agency, while also warning that fixed blueprints risk monological closure.

text.text: From an SRT perspective, this suggests that the critical issue is not only how representations change, but how temporal horizons remain open, contested, and plural.
Across applied domains, these dynamics take on normative and political dimensions.

In environmental contexts, temporal framing shapes moral engagement: representing distant risks as far away delays collective responsibility (Lee & Barnett, 2022; Uzelgun & Castro, 2014; Fischer et al., 2018).

text.text: What unifies these domains is the insight that future imaginaries are not politically neutral: they distribute responsibility, agency, and possibility unevenly across social positions.

Indeed, in colonial and environmental contexts, competing visions of progress reveal whose futures are prioritized and whose are marginalized (Cabecinhas & Brasil, 2019; Normann, 2021; Negura et al., 2020; Castro, 2014).

text.text: Despite these advances, research on the future within SRT remains more fragmented than the study of the past.
Anticipation is still frequently treated as an adjunct to anchoring or as an applied theme rather than as a representational process in its own right.

A more fully temporalized SRT would instead theorize anticipation as projectual temporality: a generative and contested capacity through which communities imagine, negotiate, and legitimize what could or should be.

In this sense, temporality should be understood not only as dialogical, but also as teleological and pragmatic, binding social representations to collective agency -and SRT as a framework uniquely equipped to explore it.
Additionally, narrative processes become particularly relevant here.

While representations of the past and present can draw on relatively stabilized reference points that carry argumentative force, future-oriented representations lack such empirical grounding and must be rendered intelligible through symbolic and narrative forms (Brescó de Luna, 2018; Jovchelovitch & Hawlina, 2018).

text.text: Anticipation therefore relies on culturally available narrative resources that organize what can be imagined, justified, and coordinated within a given representational field.

Narratives do not simply describe possible futures; they structure them by linking imagined endpoints with meaningful trajectories, thereby enabling actors to orient themselves toward what is not yet realized.

In this sense, the capacity of a future-oriented representation to circulate and gain legitimacy depends not only on its normative appeal, but also on its narrative coherence and cultural resonance (Pedersen, 2021; Wallace & Batel, 2024).

text.text: Accordingly, more coherent and symbolically familiar narratives are more easily shared, negotiated, and stabilized across social positions, shaping the competition between alternative representations of what the future could or should be.
Questions of dynamics have always been central to Social Representations Theory, which has long attended to how representations emerge, stabilize, circulate, and transform.

From Moscovici's foundational concepts of anchoring and objectification (1961, 1988) to Marková's dialogical reconceptualization of meaning-making (2003), the theory has developed a rich vocabulary for analysing processes of change and continuity.

text.text: Yet, dynamics should not be conflated with temporality: where the former describes movement and stability within time, the latter concerns how time itself is socially and symbolically constituted within the everyday sphere.
Across its diverse schools and empirical traditions, the theory embeds distinct conceptions of time, often implicitly.
Together, these perspectives illuminate how societies bind knowledge to time, yet it is primarily the genetic and dialogical traditions of SRT that treat temporality as an explicit concern.

As the review in Sections 3.1 and 3.2 demonstrates, research remains considerably more robust in explaining how the past structures the present than in accounting for how alternative futures orient collective life.

The future, when it appears, is often treated as a derivative of memory or as an implicit extension of anchoring processes, reflecting what Hartog (2003) identified as the presentist bias of modern social thought.

text.text: This imbalance is mirrored empirically: while memory, narrative, and history constitute consolidated research fields within SRT, future-oriented studies remain fragmented across applied domains such as education, climate change, or health.
Underlying this asymmetry is a deeper epistemic hierarchy, in which the known is systematically privileged over the possible.
Notwithstanding this tendency, several strands within SRT already provide the conceptual resources for a more fully temporalized theory.

Contributions such as Cinnirella's (1998) work on possible social identities, Bauer and Gaskell's (1999, 2008) projectual models, Buhagiar and Sammut's (2020) analysis of joint projects, or Wallace and Batel's (2024) regimes of future orientation demonstrate that SRT can theorise anticipation, projection, and purposive orientation. Flament's (1994) distinction between reversible and irreversible change further suggests that actors' representations of an object are shaped not only by its current state but by their projections of whether transformation can be undone.

text.text: Yet these contributions remain dispersed, functioning more as thematic incursions than as components of an integrated research programme on temporality.

To integrate them coherently, SRT must move beyond treating time as a passive backdrop and instead conceptualize temporality as constitutive of how representations are formed, contested, and transformed.

A conception of temporality grounded in the theory's own conceptual resources would therefore include how time is symbolically constructed (symbolic dimension), lived and experienced (experiential dimension), encoded through moral obligations and responsibilities (normative dimension), and distributed unequally across social positions (political dimension).

What SRT can contribute to the study of these dimensions is a framework linking temporality to the social production of common sense: that is, to how societies collectively construct, negotiate, stabilize, and contest representations of the past, present, and future through communication, conflict, and everyday meaning-making.

Building on the present review, we argue that developing this linkage within SRT requires attention to four core components through which temporality becomes empirically tractable: (1) contents, namely the representations through which groups define past, present, and future; (2) representational processes, through which temporal contents (and time itself) are anchored, objectified, and contested; (3) projects, understood as the collective orientation through which social groups assign direction, purpose, and value to represented objects; and (4) projections, referring to the imaginative extension of representations into possible futures or their retrospective reconfiguration in light of anticipated ends.
Temporal contents are present in SRT but remains underdeveloped.
As Ramos (1994) demonstrated in his lexicometric analysis, temporal categories are not arbitrary but structured lexically and semantically within shared vocabularies.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Ramos (1994)</ref> demonstrated in his lexicometric analysis, temporal categories are not arbitrary but structured lexically and semantically within shared vocabularies.

text.text: As a working definition, representations of time may be understood as the systems of values, ideas, and practices (Moscovici, 1988) through which social groups make sense of past, present, and future.
text.formatted: As a working definition, representations of time may be understood as the systems of values, ideas, and practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Moscovici, 1988)</ref> through which social groups make sense of past, present, and future.

text.text: These contents are stabilised in language (e.g. "running out of time," "timeless tradition"), embedded in everyday metaphors ("time is money," "time flies"), and enacted through social practices such as scheduling, sequencing, and ritual timing.
In this sense, temporal contents function as symbolic resources through which groups navigate uncertainty, sustain collective identities, and orient themselves toward past and future.
Crucially, however, groups do not merely represent objects in time; they also represent time itself: its pace, direction, and perceived fairness.
Temporal categories such as urgency, delay, progress, or irreversibility encode moral judgements and political claims.
Discourses of urgency in climate politics, for instance, frame responsibility and justify intervention, while bureaucratic regimes of waiting transform duration into a mode of subjection.
Affective orientations such as hope, stagnation, or inevitability operate as chronotopic configurations (Marková & Novaes, 2020), aligning collective emotions with particular temporal orders.
text.formatted: Affective orientations such as hope, stagnation, or inevitability operate as chronotopic configurations <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Marková & Novaes, 2020)</ref>, aligning collective emotions with particular temporal orders.

text.text: Temporality is thus inherently normative and political, shaping who may act, when, and with what legitimacy.
These first two facets of temporality thus contribute to the project dimension, defined as the collective and pragmatic orientation assigned to objects of representations..

Finally, we suggest adding a fourth aspect -projection-to capture the narrative and imaginative extension of representations through which groups imagine possible futures, and therefore alternative visions of past and present.
Narratives are inherently teleological, endowing past events with meaning in light of anticipated futures (Bruner, 2011; Ricoeur, 1984).

text.text: Imagined futures may retroactively reshape the past, reconfiguring what is remembered, forgotten, or silenced (Brescò de Luna, 2018).

In line with SRT scholarship on absences and silences (Barreiro & Castorina, 2016; Chokier & Moliner, 2006; Guimelli & Deschamps, 2000), attention to imagination can illuminate the moral and affective shifts that occur as societies move between inherited pasts and envisaged futures.

text.text: Each strand of SRT contains the seeds for this temporal reorientation.
Structural approaches provide a robust framework for understanding continuity but tend to treat change as reactive.
Extending them temporally entails focusing on representational tempo: the pace at which meanings migrate from periphery to core.
Peripheral elements may function as temporal incubators for alternative futures, circulating at the margins before gaining centrality.
Similarly, zones of challenge may reveal minority memories and emergent projects.
Sociodynamic approaches are particularly well suited to analysing the politics of anticipation.
Social groups possess unequal temporal agency: the power to define desirable futures, to set the pace of change, or to defer transformation.
This can be conceptualised as a form of modal power: the capacity to shape what others perceive as possible, plausible, or inevitable.

A re-temporalized sociodynamic approach could thus examine conflicts over tempo (acceleration versus delay), trajectory (growth versus degrowth), and closure (open versus foreclosed futures), revealing how status and power structure participation in imagining collective futures.
Genetic approaches already conceptualise temporality as developmental.

Extending them toward projection would allow analysis of how anticipated futures interact across scales: how shortterm discursive innovations may, through repetition and institutionalisation, reshape personal meaning systems and eventually sediment into collective representations.

At the individual level, research on time perspective (Fieulaine & Apostolidis, 2015; Lewin, 1943; Stolarski et al., 2018) offers a compatible vocabulary for examining how shared temporal orientations anchor and reproduce collective representations, providing a bridge between micro-and macro-temporal dynamics.

text.text: Finally, dialogical approaches situate temporality within ongoing interaction but often underplay hierarchies of voice and resonance.
Integrating dialogical analysis with a sensitivity to power enables questions such as: who speaks for the past, and who claims authority over the future?
In public debates on sustainability, some actors invoke ancestors, others appeal to "future generations" positioning themselves within moral chronologies of debt, inheritance, and responsibility.

Combining dialogical SRT with discourse and deliberative analysis (Hajer, 2006; Wodak, 2016) could reveal how this temporal polyphony is stratified, that is, how some futures gain legitimacy while others remain inaudible.

text.text: Cultural domains such as fiction, cinema, and online subcultures are particularly fertile sites for such analysis, functioning as representational incubators where possible futures are affectively rehearsed before they materialise (Zittoun & Gillespie, 2018).

text.text: By tracing how temporalities are anchored, objectified, and projected through narratives, practices, and artefacts -and by interrogating how power, memory, imagination, and identity condition which futures become thinkable, which pasts authoritative, and which presents appear "out of time"-SRT can move beyond its presentist bias and develop a genuinely substantive theory of temporality.
Such a re-temporalisation would remain faithful to SRT's core concern with meaning-making while recognising that meaning itself is always made in and through time.

Taken together, the review demonstrates that SRT is already, at its core, a theory deeply concerned with time, albeit one that has rarely made its temporal commitments explicit or distinguished them from the study of processual dynamics.
We mapped the temporal logics embedded within SRT, showing how each of its main approaches contains an implicit opening toward time.
Across its diverse developments, a persistent tendency remains: to treat time as a neutral container rather than a constitutive dimension of representational processes.

While the field abounds with studies that touch on temporal aspects, and while each major approach offers its own vocabulary for doing so, representations are examined primarily for how they preserve continuity with the past rather than how they open pathways to the future.

Yet, across these configurations, a gap persists within SRT between research on how representations emerge, stabilize, and transform and research on how time itself is socially and symbolically constituted within the everyday sphere.
Much of SRT's intellectual architecture is oriented toward the former.

While important developments -including the pragmatic turn initiated by Bauer and Gaskell (1999, 2008), as well as more recent work on imagination, anticipation, and creativity-have begun to address this limitation, the temporal dimensions of representational life remain underdeveloped.

text.text: By recognizing temporality as a constitutive dimension of meaning-making, SRT can move beyond the past-present dyad and engage more fully with the politics of anticipation.
This reorientation also demands attention to the symbolic meanings of time itself: its tempo, directionality, reversibility, and moral legitimacy.
Temporal categories such as speed, delay, progress and decline are not neutral descriptors but moral and political signifiers that regulate what kinds of futures are imaginable and for whom.
The "urgency" of energy transition (Uzelgun & Castro, 2014) or the "waiting" imposed on migrants (Näre et al., 2022) illustrate how temporality becomes a medium of governance and inequality.

text.text: In this sense, representations do not merely evolve in time; they actively construct temporal regimes and literacies through which social meanings are experienced, negotiated, and contested.

Building on these insights, we claim for a temporalized approach to social representations; one that treats time not as backdrop but as symbolically mediated, politically charged, and affectively experienced.
Crucially, this agenda requires developing analyses of contents, processual dynamics, projects and projection.
We are not the first to advance a temporally attentive social psychology.

Recent work within and adjacent to SRT has increasingly foregrounded anticipation, imagination, and creativity as constitutive dimensions of meaning-making (Glăveanu & Tanggaard, 2014; Power et al., 2023; see also the recently published special issue edited by Prosser et al., 2025).

text.text: For instance, building on the dialogical approach, Glăveanu and de Saint Laurent (2025) have proposed a future-oriented framework for studying horizons of possibility as embedded in social interaction and mediated by symbolic resources.

Such contributions demonstrate that SRT already possesses the conceptual apparatus to study temporality both as a content and as a generative and pragmatic process, even if these insights have yet to be fully integrated into our collective understanding of what lies within -and at the margins of-a social representations perspective.
Ultimately, our call to substantiate time within SRT is not a departure from its foundational concerns but a deepening of them.
Temporality must be theorized as plural, situated, and imaginative -that is, capable of linking memory and anticipation, sedimentation and rupture, continuity and transformation.
This plural temporality is not linear but ecological: a living network of durations through which groups orient themselves in symbolic space.
To study this ecology is to engage with the moral architectures of collective life: who is allowed to move fast, who must wait, who claims the past, and who can speak for the future.
